title: The It'll-Get-Worse-Before-It-Gets-Better Fallacy
hook: A falling line can look like proof of progress when someone promised pain first.
coreIdea: The fallacy appears when worsening conditions are treated as evidence that a plan is working, without a mechanism or reference point.
counterintuition: Some good fixes do hurt at first. The trap is using that pain as proof. A real transition can explain why things get worse, how long it should last, and what early signal should show recovery.
tryThisNow: For one struggling plan, write the promised mechanism and expected dip. Add the signal that would prove plain failure.
keyTakeaway: Worse before better is a prediction to test, not an excuse to keep believing.

breakdown.fastRead:
A control chart sits beside the hotel overbooking desk, and the red line is moving the wrong way. Nathan hears the consultant's promise again: complaints will get worse before they get better. The sentence makes the drop feel meaningful.

That is the fallacy. A plan fails, then the failure gets treated as evidence that the plan is entering its hard but necessary phase. The story protects itself by turning bad news into support.

Pain is not proof.

The useful move is to ask what mechanism should turn this pain into later gain, what time window was predicted, and what failure signal would make the plan stop.
breakdown.deepRead:
The control chart on Nathan's desk shows five nights of more walk-outs, longer lobby lines, and higher refund costs. The new overbooking model was supposed to improve revenue by accepting more reservations than rooms. The vendor warned that guests might complain at first. Now the warning is becoming a shield.

Worse before better is sometimes real. A store remodel can cut sales during construction and improve them after reopening. A new scheduling system can slow staff while they learn and then reduce errors. A training plan can feel awkward before skill improves. But in those cases, there is a mechanism: the present cost buys a later capability.

A prediction needs a fuse, not a fog bank.

Nathan writes three columns under the chart. First: what was supposed to get worse? Second: when was it supposed to turn? Third: what would count as a failure signal? The vendor named complaints but not walk-outs. It named two weeks but not rising refund costs. That gives Nathan a real decision: pause the model in two hotels and compare the old rule against the new one.

A chemicals plant incentive review shows the same excuse in a sharper setting. Fiona is holding an exam sheet for a safety quiz after near misses rise under a new bonus plan. A supervisor says the bad month was predicted. Fiona writes prediction excuse on the exam sheet and asks whether the plan had named near misses as a temporary cost or only lower production as the expected dip.

If every bad signal counts as expected pain, nothing can fail.
breakdown.fullRead:
A pediatric clinic waiting room smells of hand sanitizer and damp coats. Eric has a market memo from the scheduling vendor, a list of missed appointments, and a nurse saying parents are angrier than before. The vendor said the new default booking flow would feel rough at first. Eric writes failure signal across the memo before the next contract call.

The fallacy works because humans like meaningful pain better than pointless pain. If a difficult plan hurts, we want the hurt to mean something. The phrase worse before better offers that meaning. It turns discomfort into a badge of progress. It lets a leader sound patient, disciplined, and brave while the evidence gets worse.

Ask a harder question: what exactly is the pain buying?

If the answer is learning, then learning should be visible. If the answer is cleanup, then the backlog should shrink. If the answer is a necessary transition, then the old friction should decrease while the new friction appears. Without that link, the phrase worse before better becomes a prediction excuse. It tells you why not to update when the current evidence says update.

Eric tests the clinic memo that way. The vendor predicted more calls during the first week because parents would need help using the new portal. That part happened. But missed appointments also rose, and no one predicted that. The mechanism does not explain the failure signal. Eric keeps the portal open for families using it well, restores phone booking for the missed-appointment group, and asks for a one-week comparison.

You can feel the pull in any plan you already defended in public. You told staff the change would be hard. Now it is hard. Part of you wants to say, see, this proves we are in the hard part. But a real forecast has edges. It says which metric gets worse, which one should improve early, and when the story expires.

That expiry date matters.

A farm rainfall projection makes the trap even clearer. You are looking at a closed-door list of seed orders with Anke, the farm manager. A consultant said the new planting schedule would look worse before it gets better because early fields would be left bare. Then rainfall forecasts changed. The bare fields are no longer preparation; they may be lost yield. Anke writes therapy trap on the list and must decide whether the discomfort is still buying resilience or merely hiding a stale plan.

This is not an argument for quitting at the first sign of trouble. It is an argument for specifying trouble before it arrives. If a plan expects a dip, write the dip down. If the plan expects recovery, write the first recovery signal down. If the dip spreads into areas the plan did not predict, treat that as information.

So do not ask whether things got worse. Ask whether they got worse in the way the plan predicted, for the reason the plan named, inside the window the plan set. Anything less is a story trying to outrun the evidence.
breakdown.whyItMatters: The fallacy turns bad news into protection for a weak plan. Readers need to separate a real transition dip from an excuse that cannot be falsified.

reviewCards.front: A plan gets worse and someone says that was expected. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what mechanism links this pain to later gain, how long the dip should last, and what signal would prove failure.

reviewCards.front: Why is worse before better a dangerous phrase?
reviewCards.back: It can turn bad evidence into support for the plan unless the prediction was specific and testable.

reviewCards.front: A transition dip was predicted. What still matters?
reviewCards.back: Whether the dip matches the predicted metric, cause, and time window, and whether early recovery signals appear.
A claim that absorbs bad results by saying they were expected, without naming what would count as failure.

reviewCards.front: A painful change may be necessary. How do you keep judgment clean?
reviewCards.back: Define the expected pain and the recovery signal before the pain arrives. Then update when reality falls outside the forecast.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to separate a real transition dip from an unfalsifiable excuse by naming the mechanism, time window, and failure signal.

ifThenPlans.plan: If someone says a worsening metric was expected, then I will ask which metric was predicted to worsen and when it should turn.
If a rollout hurts one group more than expected, then I will treat that as a failure signal until the mechanism explains it.
If discomfort feels meaningful, then I will ask what useful capability the discomfort is supposed to create and how I will see it.
If a vendor explains bad results as temporary pain, then I will require a dated recovery signal before extending the contract.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, find one plan that is getting worse. Write the predicted dip, the mechanism, and the signal that would make you stop or revise it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, add an expiry date and a failure signal to one ongoing change that has been justified as temporary pain.
